messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Eduardo was sixty-seven, a widowed prosecutor who had spent decades navigating the rigid corridors of the justice system, but his clinical picture was defined by a violation that occurred three years ago. During a family gathering, a relative he had trusted had cornered him in a hotel suite, pressing him against the wall with hands that were freezing cold. That specific temperature on the skin became an immediate trigger. When he later felt that precise chill in the air of a courtroom antechamber, the traumatic event would suddenly flood back as vivid memory, the details of the assault rendered with terrifying clarity. Because the sensation bypassed his conscious guard, the memory forces its way into his mind when he does not want to, stripping away his professional composure and leaving him breathless. That sudden recall quickly reshaped his internal landscape. The violation by a trusted relative confirmed that the world is a dangerous place, while the physical intrusion led him to believe that his body has been permanently damaged by what happened. He began to view himself as fundamentally contaminated, carrying a shame that felt as inescapable as the assailant’s grip. This internal shift was brief in its initial recognition, yet it planted the seeds of his ongoing distress. His conviction of physical vulnerability and pervasive contamination soon dictated his daily navigation. Because he was certain that the world is a dangerous place, he could no longer trust his environment to protect him. Avoiding unfamiliar places because he could not assess the danger became his operating principle, leading him to restrict his professional travel to familiar district attorney offices. As soon as he entered any room or building, he would scan for exits as soon as he enter any room or building, mapping escape routes with practiced urgency. He also noticed weapons in any environment with clinical precision, his eyes automatically cataloging pens, heavy ashtrays, or broken glass that could be turned against him. The entrenched nature of these beliefs actively amplified his internal experience. What frightened him most was how his own negative appraisals primed his recall, causing his memories to surface with greater intensity whenever he doubted his safety. The contamination he felt on the inside made his mind constantly hunt for evidence that the past had irrevocably broken him, ensuring that vivid recall would not fade. This internalized fear also heightened his sensitivity to external cues. He had come to believe that his body has been permanently damaged by what happened, which made him hyperaware of any physical sensation that mirrored the original violation. Consequently, being around children now activates a wave of guilt and alarm, and he finds himself reacting to triggers far more intensely, because the appraisal that he is fundamentally compromised turns every incidental chill or casual touch into a confirmation of his ongoing peril. The vivid quality of his recall directly fueled his hypervigilance. When the memory feels present rather than past, it strips away the protective distance of time, making the threat feel immediate. This relentless present-tense recall meant that every minor stressor was filtered through a lens of anticipated violation, and he noticed weapons in any environment with urgent urgency, not as an abstract habit, but as a direct response to a mind that believed the attack was occurring again. Each involuntary intrusion also solidified his core beliefs about himself and the world. The uncontrolled access of his memories provided constant, undeniable proof to his own negative interpretations. When the memory forces its way into his mind when he does not want to, it feels like incontrovertible evidence that the world is a dangerous place. This feedback loop ensured that his appraisals of personal vulnerability and universal danger never had a chance to fade. His relentless scanning and avoidance patterns paradoxically kept the trauma alive. By constantly scanning exits as soon as he enter any room or building and avoiding going to unfamiliar places because he cannot assess the danger, he denied his nervous system the opportunity to learn that he was safe. The constant state of threat monitoring meant that his brain remained on high alert for the original assault scenario, which in turn made the memory more likely to surface. His efforts to stay safe had accidentally guaranteed that the traumatic recall would never recede. This perpetual state of danger assessment also lowered his threshold for environmental cues. He had come to believe that the world is a dangerous place, which meant his nervous system interpreted neutral stimuli as potential attacks. Because he was constantly scanning exits and noticing weapons, his baseline anxiety remained elevated, and this hyperarousal ensured that a specific temperature on the skin immediately bypassed his logic and hijacked his physiology. The threat system had essentially rewritten his sensory processing, completing the loop that tightened daily. Today, Eduardo continues to work as a prosecutor, but his courtroom routines have shrunk to the safe perimeters of familiar district attorney offices. He navigates the sterile, air-conditioned corridors deliberately, avoiding the outdoor patios where children gather for family events, knowing that being around children now triggers a wave of guilt he no longer knows how to manage. The final straw came last week during a routine case review, when a colleague accidentally bumped his shoulder with an ice pack. The chilling contact triggered the full cascade: the memory returned, his body felt irrevocably broken, and he recognized that his avoidance was isolating him from his late wife’s memory and his professional duties. He came to treatment hoping to untangle the cycle that has kept him trapped in the past, terrified that if he stops scanning for exits, he will never survive another attack.
